schools.summary: Henry refuses to let the way of all the earth be heard as a mere ending: death is a way, not only a period of this life but a passage to a better, and all who dwell on earth are themselves earth and must return to it, so that even the heirs of heaven go it, though they walk it with pleasure, and prophets and kings go it to a brighter honour than prophecy or sovereignty. He draws the chapter's sharpest distinction between the two promises, that the Messiah should come of David's loins being absolute while a man on the throne of Israel was conditional on his seed, and sums it that we never let fall the promise till we let fall the precept, the authority of a dying father being much but nothing to that of a living God.

Keil and Delitzsch reject outright the reading that be strong and show thyself a man means bear my departure bravely, holding that the courage is to show itself in obedience, since the object is appended by the copula and the phrase to keep the keeping of Jehovah always takes its sense from the context. Ellicott divides the deathbed, calling the general charge noble enough and in harmony with the last words of David on him that ruleth over men being just, with the everlasting covenant ordered in all things and sure, and with the prayer in Chronicles, so that David speaks here in the spirit of a true servant of God, while in the particular charges that follow he sees the worldly prudence of an old statesman and the trace of a long-remembered grudge, true to imperfect human nature though unworthy of an ideal hero-king.

Clarke answers the phrase from the Latin poets, quoting one of them three times on the pale death that knocks at palace and cottage with one foot and Blair on the tomb as the appointed rendezvous where all travellers meet, and makes the charge to show thyself a man a charge to act like a rational being and not a brute. Taking the five terms of the charge in order he states a position larger than the verse, that a thing is not good because God has commanded it nor evil because he has forbidden it, but that he commanded the good because it is in its own nature good and useful and forbade the evil because it is hurtful; and he follows the condition to its end, that David's seed did not keep it and the justice of God cut off the entail his mercy had made.

Gill takes the words plainly as the path none are exempted from, kings or peasants, and adds a dating inference of his own, that David seems to have borrowed the phrase from Joshua, which shows that book was written in his day. He reports from his Jewish authorities that the dying man is called only David and not King David, either because Solomon was already anointed and reigning in his stead or because no man, not even a king, has power in the day of death, having no rule over it while it rules over him.

debates: What be strong and show thyself a man requires: Keil and Delitzsch deny it means bearing the king's death bravely and make it courage in obedience, Clarke makes it acting like a rational being rather than a brute, Henry makes it resolution in one who was a man in years but a child, Ellicott simply manhood in spite of youth

Whether the deathbed charge is admirable: Ellicott divides it, the general part noble and spoken in the spirit of a saint, the particular charges showing an old statesman's worldly prudence and a remembered grudge

How the promise to David stands: Henry distinguishes an absolute promise of the Messiah from a conditional promise of a man on the throne, Clarke observes that the condition failed and justice cut off the entail, Keil and Delitzsch read the everlasting possession of the throne as still to be fulfilled to Solomon
outliers: Clarke states a general position on law, that a thing is not good because God commanded it nor evil because he forbade it, but that he commanded the good because it is good in its own nature
Gill infers from David's use of Joshua's phrase that the book of Joshua was written in David's day
Gill reports the rabbinic observation that the dying king is called only David, since no man has power in the day of death
Clarke answers the way of all the earth from Horace and from Blair's poem on the grave rather than from Scripture
themes: death as a way and not a period
a charge to be strong in obedience
an absolute promise and a conditional one
a deathbed divided against itself
1.pericope_label: Now the days of David drew nigh that he should die; and he charged Solomon his son, saying, I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man; And keep the charge of the Lord thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself: That the Lord may continue his word which he spake concerning me, saying, If thy children take heed to their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail thee (said he) a man on the throne of Israel.

schools.summary: Clarke is the most absolute on Joab, holding that it would have been an insult to justice not to take his life, that David was culpable in delaying so long, that by the law of God a man who had murdered Abner and Amasa must die, and that had David not laid the duty on Solomon he could not have died in the approbation of his Maker. On Shimei he reverses the sentence by a point of grammar, arguing that the negative in hold him not guiltless should be understood again in the clause that follows, as Hebrew often repeats a particle without expressing it, so that the charge reads bring thou not down his hoary head to the grave with blood. He reports the tradition of treasure buried with David and plundered centuries later, gives it little credit, and dismisses the modern show of the tomb.

Ellicott grants the Joab charge a certain righteousness, since David could not and dared not punish him as he deserved, and finds in the blood of war shed in peace a vividness showing how the horror dwelt on his imagination; but he weighs Abner's murder as having some show of justification in the duty of the avenger of blood while Amasa's was plain revenge, judges the punishment just and within the letter of the law though clemency might have spared an old warrior, calls the Shimei charge the most ungenerous of all and a virtual withdrawal of a pardon, and observes that David says nothing of the act he most likely resented, the slaughter of Absalom. Keil and Delitzsch resolve the Shimei difficulty by distinguishing the personal forgiveness David had given from the insult offered to the anointed of the Lord as representative of the rights of God, which he could not forgive, and note that punishing so powerful a man as the commander-in-chief required wisdom if the army devoted to him was not to rebel.

Henry defends the Shimei charge on the narrow ground that it proceeded not from personal revenge but from a prudent zeal for the honour of the government and the covenant God had made with the house, adding that a hoary head, if guilty and forfeited, ought not to be any man's protection from justice; and on Barzillai he holds that kindnesses received must not be buried in our friends' graves or our own but returned by our children to theirs.

Gill observes that David slept with his fathers without being buried with them, so that the phrase means the state of the dead rather than the grave, and dates the death and the reign from his Jewish and classical authorities.

debates: Whether the charges against Joab and Shimei are justice or vendetta: Clarke holds it would have been an insult to justice to spare Joab and that David erred only in delay, Henry defends the Shimei charge as zeal for the government and not private revenge, Keil and Delitzsch distinguish a personal pardon from an unforgivable insult to the Lord's anointed, and Ellicott calls the Shimei charge the most ungenerous of all and hears an old grudge rankling in it

What the charge about Shimei actually said: Clarke argues that the Hebrew repeats the negative without expressing it, so that David forbade rather than commanded the bringing down of his hoary head with blood
outliers: Ellicott notes that David says nothing of the act he most probably resented most, the reckless slaughter of Absalom against his express command, nor alludes to Joab's recent treason
Keil and Delitzsch read do according to thy wisdom as marking the proper opportunity, since the army was devoted to its commander and a rebellion had to be avoided
Clarke dismisses the shown tomb of David on the ground that monks and Mohammedans have long united to impose on pilgrims
themes: justice owed and gratitude owed
a pardon that bound the father only
blood of war shed in peace
a reign of forty years closed
5.pericope_label: Moreover thou knowest also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, and what he did to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, unto Abner the son of Ner, and unto Amasa the son of Jether, whom he slew, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of war upon his girdle that was about his loins, and in his shoes that were on his feet. Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace. But shew kindness unto the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be of those that eat at thy table: for so they came to me when I fled because of Absalom thy brother. And, behold, thou hast with thee Shimei the son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim, which cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim: but he came down to meet me at Jordan, and I sware to him by the Lord, saying, I will not put thee to death with the sword. Now therefore hold him not guiltless: for thou art a wise man, and knowest what thou oughtest to do unto him; but his hoar head bring thou down to the grave with blood. So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David. And the days that David reigned over Israel were forty years: seven years reigned he in Hebron, and thirty and three years reigned he in Jerusalem.

schools.summary: Henry calls the suit a treasonable project, Adonijah seeking Abishag not out of love but because by her he hoped to renew his claim, or because holding a predecessor's wives was then reckoned a branch of the government, as Absalom had thought his pretensions supported by lying with his father's concubines; it was a small game, but he hoped to make it an after-game for the kingdom and to gain by a wife what he could not gain by force. The execution he judges just and necessary, Adonijah betraying himself into the hands of Solomon's justice while the righteous God left him to himself, and he warns that many ruin themselves because they do not know when they are well done to. The honour shown Bathsheba he reads as obedience to the fifth commandment, children grown great owing honour to their parents no less than children merely grown up.

Ellicott reaches the same suspicion of the petition by custom rather than motive, since by Eastern usage to take a king's wives was the known privilege of his successor, which is why Ahithophel gave Absalom that unseemly but politic counsel, so that a public espousal of Abishag might have passed for a renewed claim, and he remarks that Solomon sees this at once though Bathsheba strangely does not. On the execution he is divided, granting the policy but hearing in Solomon's answer a bitterness venting itself in irony which argues passionate feeling mingled with kingly dignity, not unlike his father's bursts over Nabal, and noting that the king infers the hand of the conspirators, rightly or wrongly, and executes vengeance summarily without granting a trial. He explains the deference paid Bathsheba from the standing of a queen mother in Eastern monarchies, and finds the comparison of Solomon's oath with David's characteristic, since in David we always see the living man whose soul longs after God while Solomon is emphatically the king, his individual character almost merged in the majesty of his royalty.

Clarke denies the design altogether, holding that it does not appear Adonijah had any thought of the kingdom in the request however Solomon understood him, and that without further evidence this was a flimsy pretext to imbrue his hands in a brother's blood, the fable of the wolf and the lamb applying, and the proverb that it is an easy thing to find a staff to beat a dog with. He refuses the execution as cruelty needing no proof, the man being suspected, condemned and slain without a hearing, and turns on a commentator who defended it on the ground that a prince cannot always follow the rules of the most perfect morality, calling the maxim diabolical and remarking that if that is how French kings ruled the revolution is no wonder. Behind the whole dispute he sets the right of God, whose kingdom it was and whose lieutenants the kings were, and who was pleased to give the crown to Solomon.

debates: What the request for Abishag meant: Henry makes it a treasonable project aimed at renewing the claim, Ellicott finds a covert design in the Eastern custom by which a successor took the king's wives, and Clarke denies that Adonijah had any thought of the kingdom in it at all

Whether the execution was just: Henry calls it just and necessary and has Adonijah betray himself, Ellicott grants the policy but notes that vengeance was executed summarily without trial and with a bitterness that argues passion, and Clarke calls it cruelty needing no proof and names anyone who defends it by state necessity or divine command an enemy to the cause of God and truth
outliers: Clarke attacks a commentator's maxim that a prince cannot always follow the rules of the most perfect morality, calls it diabolical, and connects such government with the French revolution
Ellicott contrasts David and Solomon through their oaths, the one always the living man whose soul longs after God, the other emphatically the king whose individual character is merged in his royalty
Ellicott thinks Solomon's irony gives some probability to the conjecture that Abishag was the Shulamite of the Song, already loved by the young king
themes: a petition with a crown inside it
a queen mother between two sons
vengeance without a hearing
the right of God above every title
12.pericope_label: Then sat Solomon upon the throne of David his father; and his kingdom was established greatly. And Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bath–sheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, Comest thou peaceably? And he said, Peaceably. He said moreover, I have somewhat to say unto thee. And she said, Say on. And he said, Thou knowest that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign: howbeit the kingdom is turned about, and is become my brother’s: for it was his from the Lord. And now I ask one petition of thee, deny me not. And she said unto him, Say on. And he said, Speak, I pray thee, unto Solomon the king, (for he will not say thee nay,) that he give me Abishag the Shunammite to wife. And Bath–sheba said, Well; I will speak for thee unto the king. Bath–sheba therefore went unto king Solomon, to speak unto him for Adonijah. And the king rose up to meet her, and bowed himself unto her, and sat down on his throne, and caused a seat to be set for the king’s mother; and she sat on his right hand. Then she said, I desire one small petition of thee; I pray thee, say me not nay. And the king said unto her, Ask on, my mother: for I will not say thee nay. And she said, Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah thy brother to wife. And king Solomon answered and said unto his mother, And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also; for he is mine elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah. Then king Solomon sware by the Lord, saying, God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah have not spoken this word against his own life. Now therefore, as the Lord liveth, which hath established me, and set me on the throne of David my father, and who hath made me an house, as he promised, Adonijah shall be put to death this day. And king Solomon sent by the hand of Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell upon him that he died.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the handling of Abiathar as proof how free Solomon's actions were from personal revenge or excessive severity, the priest having forfeited his life in the conspiracy yet being merely sent to his fields at Anathoth and told he would not die that day because he had borne the ark, which is to say because of his high-priestly dignity; they also insist that Joab fled not to the tabernacle but to the holy tent upon Zion, and reject as an arbitrary rendering the attempt to alter the text so as to read Solomon for Absalom. Ellicott denies precisely their account of the pardon, holding that it is not Abiathar's priestly character which protects him but the remembrance of his long friendship to David in adversity; he is careful that the words about fulfilling the prophecy describe the effect and not the purpose of Solomon's action, and makes the chapter's sharpest legal observation, that the sentence on Joab mentions nothing but the old murders, possibly so as to bring the case within the declaration of the Law that no sanctuary shall protect the wilful murderer.

Clarke says the priesthood thus reverted to its ancient channel, and takes the occasion for the law of sanctuary itself, that altars were so sacred almost any wretch who reached one found safety, which led to abuse and the perversion of justice until it became a maxim that the guilty be punished even from the altar, God himself decreeing that the presumptuous murderer be dragged thence; the heathen, he adds, had the same ordinance, and he quotes Euripides to the effect that he would drag an unrighteous suppliant from the altar without fearing the gods. Of the end he is plainest, that Joab bleeds now for Abner, for Amasa and for Uriah, having done the state much service but being a murderer whom vengeance would not suffer to live.

Gill is interested in who had the power to depose a high priest, insisting that it was done by Solomon's authority as king and not as a prophet, against one Roman controversialist who distinguishes so, and not by a college of priests at the king's instance, as another had claimed, for which there is no foundation; he places Joab's flight at Gibeon and has Benaiah go up to that great high place, and notes that Joab was buried in his own sepulchre and not by the altar.

debates: Why Abiathar was spared: Keil and Delitzsch say it was his high-priestly dignity, since he had borne the ark, while Ellicott denies that his priestly character protected him at all and puts it down to his long friendship to David in adversity and a promise David had made him
Where Joab took sanctuary: Keil and Delitzsch are explicit that it was the holy tent upon Zion and not the tabernacle, while Gill places it at Gibeon and Ellicott allows Gibeon as probable

Why the sentence on Joab names only the old murders: Ellicott suggests it was to bring the case within the law denying sanctuary to the wilful and treacherous murderer, rather than to punish the treason that was the real motive
outliers: Gill argues against two Roman authorities that the deposition of a high priest lay within a king's own authority and needed no college of priests
Clarke supports the forfeiture of sanctuary from Euripides, who would drag an unrighteous suppliant from the altar without fearing the wrath of the gods
Ellicott finds it significant of a monarchy grown stronger that the old captain once too hard for David fell without one act of resistance or a word spoken for him
themes: a pardon and its real ground
the word against the house of Eli fulfilled
sanctuary forfeited by murder
a captain who fell without resistance
26.pericope_label: And unto Abiathar the priest said the king, Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou art worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the Lord God before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted. So Solomon thrust out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord; that he might fulfil the word of the Lord, which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. Then tidings came to Joab: for Joab had turned after Adonijah, though he turned not after Absalom. And Joab fled unto the tabernacle of the Lord, and caught hold on the horns of the altar. And it was told king Solomon that Joab was fled unto the tabernacle of the Lord; and, behold, he is by the altar. Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, Go, fall upon him. And Benaiah came to the tabernacle of the Lord, and said unto him, Thus saith the king, Come forth. And he said, Nay; but I will die here. And Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me. And the king said unto him, Do as he hath said, and fall upon him, and bury him; that thou mayest take away the innocent blood, which Joab shed, from me, and from the house of my father. And the Lord shall return his blood upon his own head, who fell upon two men more righteous and better than he, and slew them with the sword, my father David not knowing thereof, to wit, Abner the son of Ner, captain of the host of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the host of Judah. Their blood shall therefore return upon the head of Joab, and upon the head of his seed for ever: but upon David, and upon his seed, and upon his house, and upon his throne, shall there be peace for ever from the Lord. So Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up, and fell upon him, and slew him: and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.

schools.summary: Henry makes the confinement mercy and test together, since Solomon knows how to distinguish crimes and criminals and though not bound by his father's promise will not go directly against it, keeping Shimei from the country seat where he might make mischief and holding him at Jerusalem as a prisoner at large, in a city beautiful for situation with no reason to complain of such a paradise; it was a fair trial of obedience on easy terms, and even those who perish cannot but own such conditions of pardon unexceptionable, so that their blood rests on their own heads. In Zadok's elevation he sees the threat against the house of Eli fulfilled and the promise of a faithful priest with a sure house, drawing from it that sacred offices may be disgraced but not destroyed by the maladministration of those entrusted with them.

Ellicott concedes the precaution and then takes it apart: the command was reasonable in itself against treason in a man already powerful and of doubtful fidelity, and the mention of the Kedron shows it aimed at preventing his return to Bahurim, but in the face of David's charge it is difficult to doubt it was in some degree meant as a snare, and Solomon's own closing words confirm it. The narrative gives no hint that the journey to Gath was anything but good faith to recover slaves, and a command justified by the danger of his living among his own people could hardly be disobeyed in spirit by a temporary journey abroad; so that legally the execution was defensible and may have been politic, but cannot stand examination on the ground of equity or generosity.

Clarke agrees that giving Shimei the whole city for a prison could have reduced him to no hardships, and that a seditious man at large might do much evil and was better kept under the king's eye; he marvels that with his eyes wide open the man would run into the jaws of death. He returns to his reading of David's charge and argues it now from conduct rather than grammar, that Solomon did not kill Shimei in consequence of it but confined him for life, which is the best interpretation of the text and clears David of commanding a death he had sworn not to inflict. He thinks Solomon judged that while such men went unpunished the nation could not prosper.

Gill offers a string of possible reasons for the journey, passion with his servants, haste, a covetous temper, forgetfulness, a guess that Solomon had forgotten, a hope of going and returning secretly, or a reckoning that no king would exact death for so small a fault, and settles it on providence, God leaving him to his own lust that he might suffer for cursing David; he adds that the king learned of it by the watch he had set.

debates: Whether the confinement was mercy or a snare: Henry calls it a fair trial of obedience on easy terms in a city no man could complain of, Clarke that it could have reduced him to no hardships, while Ellicott judges that in the face of David's charge it is difficult to doubt it was in some degree meant as a trap

Whether the journey to Gath was a real breach: Ellicott holds the narrative gives no hint it was other than good faith to recover slaves and that the spirit of the command was not broken, Gill accounts for it by passion, covetousness or forgetfulness under providence, Clarke only marvels at the folly
How David's charge about Shimei is to be read: Clarke argues from Solomon's own conduct, confinement rather than execution, that the charge forbade the violent death
outliers: Ellicott concludes that the execution was legally defensible and perhaps politic but cannot stand examination on the ground of equity or generosity
Ellicott notes that the Hebrew text names no successor at all to Benaiah's former command over the body-guard
Henry draws from Zadok's elevation that sacred offices may be disgraced but never destroyed by the maladministration of those entrusted with them
themes: a city for a prison
an oath forfeited at the Kedron
providence leaving a man to his own lust
a kingdom established in the hand of Solomon
35.pericope_label: And the king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada in his room over the host: and Zadok the priest did the king put in the room of Abiathar. And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Build thee an house in Jerusalem, and dwell there, and go not forth thence any whither. For it shall be, that on the day thou goest out, and passest over the brook Kidron, thou shalt know for certain that thou shalt surely die: thy blood shall be upon thine own head. And Shimei said unto the king, The saying is good: as my lord the king hath said, so will thy servant do. And Shimei dwelt in Jerusalem many days. And it came to pass at the end of three years, that two of the servants of Shimei ran away unto Achish son of Maachah king of Gath. And they told Shimei, saying, Behold, thy servants be in Gath. And Shimei arose, and saddled his ass, and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants: and Shimei went, and brought his servants from Gath. And it was told Solomon that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and was come again. And the king sent and called for Shimei, and said unto him, Did I not make thee to swear by the Lord, and protested unto thee, saying, Know for a certain, on the day thou goest out, and walkest abroad any whither, that thou shalt surely die? and thou saidst unto me, The word that I have heard is good. Why then hast thou not kept the oath of the Lord, and the commandment that I have charged thee with? The king said moreover to Shimei, Thou knowest all the wickedness which thine heart is privy to, that thou didst to David my father: therefore the Lord shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head; And king Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the Lord for ever. So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; which went out, and fell upon him, that he died. And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
